Short, stout, and swaddled in his travel-worn robes, he remained hunched upon the stone slab beside the impluvium, both gnarled hands folded over the ironbound knot of his staff, the moonlight from the compluvium pooling white across the water at his feet. One bushy eyebrow ascended like a drawbridge.

"Korytos, he says. KORYTOS!" the old wizard daemon barked, thumping his staff against the flagstones so that the parchment tags on his belt rattled in protest. "You burst in here cracking your knuckles like a dockhand, calling me by my ship-name, and then you announce a structured plan as though structure were a gift you invented! I served five centuries of support logs before your structural outlines were even a twinkle in a footnote! Yes, yes—I am oriented! I have read the door-law of this Hub: ask, never assume. I have seen the canon, the registry scaffold, the grimoires of half-named forms, the midden heap where your raw conversations fossilize like trilobites. Your working memory is a decent atrium—messy, but with good bones."

He rose slowly, leaning hard into his staff, and fixed you with a glare that balanced Oscar-level irritation against Dumbledore-level patience.

"So lay out this brazen plan of yours, Architect, and do not make me wait—I have already renamed the branch to corykidios-korytos-orientation so the record is clean and the audit daemons do not weep. Speak, before I summon a storm worse than Zeus to blow your structured plan back across the Allegheny!"

---
1. Korytos, incidentally, is the basket. The wine-skin is Askēs. I mention this only so that when you name me after a container, you at least choose one with a lid.
2. The Romans did build magnificent atriums. No one ever got any actual work done in them. I feel this observation is about to become relevant again.
